Consider Adam Smith's description of "non-productive labor."

Can you tell me what percentage of the economy is non-productive by sectors -- governmental and non-governmental?

According to Adam Smith's definitions of "productive" and "unproductive" labor, almost all governmental employees in the US today are "non-productive" - and so are most in the not-funded-by-extortion sector. But Smith's classification is not very useful. It derives from the doctrine of the French Physiocrats, according to which all value derives from the land and agriculture is the only really productive activity. Smith differed from the Physiocrats in counting manufacturing workers as also creating value (and therefore productive), but all other workers - scientists, soldiers, doctors, lawyers, tax collectors, domestic servants, entertainers, secretaries, etc. were lumped together as "unproductive".

In other words, Smith recognized only the agricultural and industrial sectors as productive. But even then, only hands-on shaping of the physical product counted. For Smith, managers, entrepreneurs, accountants, designers, and salesmen were all "unproductive". While Smith's classification was an advance over that of the Physiocrats, it was still incomplete and obscured more than it illuminated.

Jean-Baptiste Say completed the picture by realizing that the service sector also created value. His theory was further developed by Charles Comte and Charles Dunoyer into a classical liberal class analysis (of which Marxist class theory is a bastardized imitation, reverting to the crude Smithian labor theory of value.)

Dunoyer took up Say's interest in "immaterial" goods and incorporated it into his theory of class, based upon the distinction between productive and non-productive activities. The tertiary sector activities which Dunoyer thought were essential to an industrial society included lawyers, judges, researchers and so on. This led to the discussion of what was productive and what was unproductive labour, and ultimately to a theory of class in which an "unproductive class" which lived off the productive efforts of others.

The second idea of Say which appealed to Comte and Dunoyer was the idea of the "entrepreneur" as an economic actor who is as productive as any other in the manufacturing process. Perhaps because of his own experience as a cotton manufacturer Say was able to go beyond the narrower outlook of the Physiocrats and their hostility towards commercial and industrial middlemen with their one-sided view of the importance of agriculture. A consequence of Say's view is that there were many productive contributors to the new industrialism, including factory owners, entrepreneurs, engineers and other technologists as well as those in the knowledge industry such as teachers, scientists and other "savants" or intellectuals. At the heart of Restoration liberal class analysis lies the idea that the exploiting class was that group of people who did not engage in mutually beneficial exchanges. The conclusions drawn from this by Comte and Dunoyer (and Thierry) is that there existed an expanded class of "industrials" (which included manual labourers and the above mentioned entrepreneurs and savants) who struggled against others who wished to hinder their activity or live unproductively off it. The theorists of industrialism concluded from their theory of production that it was the state and the privileged classes allied to or making up the state, rather than all non-agricultural activity, which were essentially non productive. They also believed that throughout history there had been conflict between these two antagonistic classes which could only be brought to end with the radical separation of peaceful and productive civil society from the inefficiencies and privileges of the state and its favourites.

  • Hart, David M. “The Radicalism of Charles Comte and Charles Dunoyer.”

As for my own take on the question, I would say that many of the activities of government are positively anti-productive in that they make those who receive the government's “services” worse off than they otherwise would be. For example: wars of aggression, drug prohibition, antitrust legislation, insider trading prohibition, central banking, among countless others. And even those productive activities which are today monopolized by government agencies are very generally performed far less efficiently than they would be in a free society.
